pages.title: About the firm
pages.content:
Calder & Vane was founded in 1987 by two attorneys who believed that ordinary people deserve the same careful advice as large companies. We still work from the same brick building on Wharf Street, and we still answer our own phones.

What you can expect

  • A written estimate before any work begins, and no surprises on the invoice.
  • A named attorney who returns calls within one working day.
  • Plain explanations of your options, including the option of doing nothing.
  • Evening appointments on Thursdays and video meetings on request.

Community

Every attorney gives at least forty hours a year to the community legal clinic, and the firm funds two scholarships for first-generation law students at the city college.

posts.title: Can my landlord keep my security deposit?
posts.excerpt: Most deposits must be returned in full, minus documented damage beyond normal wear and tear. Here is how to get yours back.
posts.content:
Moving out is stressful enough without a fight over money you already paid. The good news is that the law is largely on the tenant's side: a deposit is your money, held as security, and the landlord has to justify every dollar they keep.

What a landlord may deduct

  • Unpaid rent or utility bills that the lease made your responsibility.
  • Damage beyond normal wear and tear, such as holes in walls or broken fixtures.
  • Cleaning costs, but only to return the home to the condition it was in when you moved in.

Faded paint, worn carpet in walkways and small nail holes for pictures are usually wear and tear. A landlord who deducts for them is on weak ground.

Deadlines matter

In most places the landlord must return the deposit, or send an itemised list of deductions, within a fixed number of days after you leave. If they miss that deadline, many statutes let the tenant claim the deposit back plus a penalty.

Photograph every room on the day you move in and the day you move out. Those photos win more deposit disputes than any lawyer.

Helena Varga-Lind

If the landlord will not pay

  1. Write a short, polite letter asking for the deposit and citing the deadline.
  2. Keep copies of the lease, the check-in report and your photos.
  3. If there is no answer within two weeks, small-claims court is usually quick and inexpensive.

If the amount is large or the landlord is a company with lawyers of its own, a short consultation can tell you whether a letter from us would settle it.

posts.title: What to do in the first 48 hours after a car accident
posts.excerpt: A short checklist for the hours after a collision, when shock makes it easy to forget the steps that protect your claim.
posts.content:
Nobody plans for a collision, and in the minutes afterwards almost everyone feels shaken. That is exactly when the details that decide an injury claim are easiest to lose. Keep this list somewhere you can find it.

At the scene

  • Check for injuries and call emergency services if anyone is hurt.
  • Move to safety if you can, and switch on hazard lights.
  • Exchange names, licence plates and insurance details with the other driver.
  • Photograph the vehicles, the road, any signs and any visible injuries.
  • Ask witnesses for a phone number. Most are happy to help, but few wait around.

Within two days

See a doctor, even if you feel fine. Some injuries, particularly to the neck and back, only show themselves a day or two later, and a medical record made early is strong evidence.

Report the accident to your insurer, but stick to the facts. You do not need to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, and you should not accept an early settlement offer before you know how badly you are hurt.

The first offer is almost never the right one. It arrives before anyone knows what your recovery will cost.

Tomas Achterberg

If someone else was at fault and you were injured, we can review your case for free. Our injury work is on a no-win, no-fee basis, so you will never pay us out of your own pocket.

comments.content: Printed this and put it in the glove box. Thank you.

posts.title: Do I really need a will if I don't own much?
posts.excerpt: A will is less about money than about decisions: who looks after your children, who sorts out your affairs and who gets the things that matter.
posts.content:
We hear this question every week, usually from people in their thirties with a rented flat, a car and some savings. The honest answer is that a will is not really about how much you own. It is about who decides what happens next.

What happens without one

If you die without a will, the law decides who inherits, in a fixed order that may not match your wishes. Unmarried partners, stepchildren and close friends are often left out entirely.

Three reasons to write one now

  1. Children. A will lets you name a guardian for children under 18.
  2. Partners. If you are not married, a will is often the only way to provide for your partner.
  3. Executors. You choose the person who will sort out your affairs, rather than leaving it to whoever applies.

A simple will

For most people with straightforward wishes. Usually one meeting and a fixed fee.

A will with a trust

For young children, blended families or someone who needs support managing an inheritance.

Whatever you choose, review it after marriage, divorce, a new child or a move abroad. A will that was right ten years ago may be wrong today.

posts.title: Fired without warning: when is a dismissal unfair?
posts.excerpt: Being dismissed suddenly is a shock, but not every dismissal is lawful. These are the questions we ask first.
posts.content:
A sudden dismissal can feel final, but the law asks more of employers than many people expect. Whether a dismissal was unfair usually depends on three things: the reason, the process and the timing.

The reason

Employers can dismiss for conduct, capability, redundancy or a handful of other fair reasons. They cannot dismiss because you raised a safety concern, took protected leave, joined a union or reported wrongdoing.

The process

  • Were you told what the problem was, in writing?
  • Were you given a chance to respond, and to bring a colleague?
  • Were you offered an appeal?

A fair reason handled with an unfair process can still make the dismissal unlawful.

Write down everything you remember about the dismissal meeting the same day: who was there, what was said and what you were handed.

Tomas Achterberg

Watch the clock

Claims usually have short time limits, sometimes only three months from the date of dismissal. If you think something was wrong, take advice early, even if you are not sure you want to make a claim.

posts.title: Divorce without a courtroom: how mediation works
posts.excerpt: Most separating couples never see a judge. Mediation is quicker, cheaper and usually kinder, especially when there are children.
posts.content:
Television makes divorce look like a courtroom drama. In reality, the large majority of separating couples settle their arrangements by agreement, and mediation is one of the most reliable ways to get there.

What a mediator does

A mediator is a neutral, trained professional who helps both of you discuss money, property and arrangements for the children. They do not take sides or make decisions; they keep the conversation productive and make sure nothing important is forgotten.

A typical timeline

Mediation is not right for everyone. Where there has been abuse or one person is hiding assets, we will advise a different route.

The best outcome for children is two parents who can still talk to each other in five years' time.

Helena Varga-Lind

posts.title: Five clauses every freelance contract should have
posts.excerpt: A one-page agreement prevents most freelance disputes. These five clauses do the heavy lifting.
posts.content:
Most disputes between freelancers and clients are not about bad faith. They come from a missing sentence: nobody wrote down when payment was due, or what counted as finished. A short written agreement fixes most of that.

  1. Scope. What you will deliver, and what you will not.
  2. Payment terms. Amount, due date and what happens if payment is late.
  3. Revisions. How many rounds are included before extra fees apply.
  4. Ownership. When the client owns the work, usually on full payment.
  5. Ending the contract. How either side can end it, and what is paid for work done so far.

Keep it readable

A contract does not need to be long to be enforceable. Plain sentences that both sides understand are more useful than pages of boilerplate nobody reads.

We offer a fixed-fee review of freelance and small-business templates. Bring the one you use today and we will tell you what is missing.

posts.title: Noise, fences and trees: settling disputes with neighbours
posts.excerpt: Neighbour disputes are rarely about the fence. A calm, staged approach settles most of them without a lawsuit.
posts.content:
A leaning fence, a tree that blocks the light, music at two in the morning: neighbour disputes are small on paper and enormous in daily life. They are also some of the hardest cases to win in court, which is why we start elsewhere.

Start with a conversation

Most people do not know they are causing a problem. A friendly conversation, followed by a short note summarising what you agreed, resolves more disputes than any letter from a lawyer.

If that does not work

  1. Check the title documents to see who owns the boundary.
  2. Keep a simple diary of noise or nuisance, with dates and times.
  3. Ask your local council about community mediation, which is often free.
  4. Only then consider a formal letter or a claim.

Remember that you will still live next door when the dispute is over.

Nadia Okonkwo-Reyes

posts.title: What happens at a free consultation (and what to bring)
posts.excerpt: Thirty to forty-five minutes, no obligation and no invoice. Here is how to get the most out of it.
posts.content:
Many people put off seeing a lawyer because they are worried about the cost of the first meeting. At our firm the first consultation is free, and there is no obligation to instruct us afterwards.

Before the meeting

  • Write a short timeline of what happened, with dates if you have them.
  • Gather letters, contracts, photos, emails and anything with a deadline.
  • Note the outcome you would like. It is fine if you are not sure yet.

During the meeting

The attorney will listen first, then ask questions. By the end you should understand your options, the likely costs and the risks of each route, including the route of doing nothing.

If we are not the right firm for your matter, we will say so and suggest who might be.
